pr_title: JIT: Validate loop invariant base case as part of IV analysis
pr_body:
Move the validation of the base case of the IV analysis into `FlowGraphNaturalLoop::AnalyzeIteration`. Previously the validation for the base case was left up to the users:

- Loop cloning tried to accomplish this by checking whether loop inversion had run, but this is not sufficient (#96623) as nothing guarantees the loop is dominated by the inverted test. Loop cloning also skipped the check entirely for GDV, leading to #95315.

- Unrolling completely neglected to check the condition leading to #96591. Furthermore, unrolling made implicit assumptions that any `BBJ_COND` init block was an inverted test and downright removed the condition without any checks. This also led to another issue #97040 where unrolling could uncover new natural loops that had not been canonicalized.

This change makes `FlowGraphNaturalLoop::AnalyzeIteration` try to prove that the loop invariant it returns is true in the base case as well as being maintained by the loop. If it cannot prove this then it fails. This fixes all the issues, but sadly uncovers that we were doing a lot of cloning in OSR methods without actually proving legality, and where it is actually illegal. We no longer clone in these cases, but we can look into what to do about them separately.

In addition, loop unrolling no longer removes the init block condition. We leave that up to RBO which is able to remove the trivial checks that loop inversion sometimes creates in generality. This does lead to a few diffs from removing the check later in the JIT pipeline.

Diffs expected from less cloning in OSR and from leaving the trivial inverted tests around until RBO.

Fix #95315
Fix #96591
Fix #96623
Fix #97040

issue_context.title: JIT: Improper zero-trip checking in loop cloning/unrolling
comments:
cc @dotnet/jit-contrib @AndyAyersMS. Likely the only remedy to get the loop cloning back for OSR cases will be to insert the entry branch later in the JIT, e.g. right before lowering, so that we retain all the context of surrounding IR during optimizations. ~~I suppose it might also be possible to place the patchpoints in a way that the zero-trip test happens at the beginning after an OSR transition, instead of at the end~~ (probably not, e.g. case below needs a zero-trip test for the outer loop but the patch point is for an inner loop). Otherwise we simply do not have the context during loop cloning in these OSR cases to be able to prove that the loop invariant is true during the first iteration.

https://github.com/dotnet/performance/blob/49d4de8e6c45036b902be1eea9bb90b63b7657fb/src/benchmarks/micro/runtime/Benchstones/BenchI/BubbleSort2.cs#L16-L27
is one example where the OSR case is doing 'unproven' loop cloning right now; we eliminate the bounds check on `x[i]` without knowing that `i <= limit1` in the first iteration.

I was trying to repro the failure on 8.0 but couldn't. Is this new behavior in 9.0? Does it require low OSR thresholds? I'll have to look more closely at how the flow graph evolves.

If we decide we need to defer changing flow until even later we need to be careful that we haven't done any **other** optimizations that would then become invalid. I think the list starts to grow.

> I was trying to repro the failure on 8.0 but couldn't. Is this new behavior in 9.0? Does it require low OSR thresholds? I'll have to look more closely at how the flow graph evolves.
> 
> If we decide we need to defer changing flow until even later we need to be careful that we haven't done any **other** optimizations that would then become invalid. I think the list starts to grow.

The example program fails with `DOTNET_TieredCompilation=0` (no OSR necessary), but when fixing it I've noticed that it is going to result in a number of OSR regressions.  The case was itself inspired by the flow in the OSR version of the BubbleSort2 example linked above.

It definitely seems hard to defer the flow change more, we would also need to make sure we checked the loop cloning conditions before jumping into one of the two versions of cloned loops. That doesn't really seem feasible. So it seems like the only thing we can do is teach loop cloning to handle the extra cases produced by OSR, for example by duplicating the zero-trip test itself as part of the choice conditions.
